t.en: A row of posts of different heights. Pick some from left to right so that each is taller than the one before; you may skip posts in between. What is the most you can pick?
Each cell records: ending with this post, the longest run you can make. The answer for the whole row is the largest cell in the row.

Look only at the last post: which post comes before it? It can be any earlier post, as long as it is shorter. However many posts come before, that is how many ways in there may be. That is exactly the sweep arm’s job: it brings in every earlier cell (the answer recorded under each post) at once.

Treat the “S” cell on the far left as a post shorter than all the others, holding 0: coming after it means this post is the first. This machine’s sweep arm has a filter: it keeps only the posts shorter than this one, and the cells it drops are dimmed in the view.

goal.en: Pick posts from left to right, each taller than the last (skipping is allowed). For each post, work out the longest run that ends with it; the answer for the row is the largest of these.

how.en: This level checks the whole row. The sweep arm only brings in posts shorter than this one; the cells it filters out are dimmed.

body.en: This cell’s ways in are no longer one or two fixed cells, but every earlier cell that meets the condition, and how many there are depends on the data.

This problem is called the <wiki-ref to="lis"></wiki-ref>: the most days you can pick from a run of share prices with each day higher than the last, or the longest upgrade path through a pile of versions, both come down to it.

note.en: The way in can be a whole run: take the max over the cells of every shorter post, then + 1.

hints.en: This post can follow any post shorter than it: click the sweep arm, and it brings in only the posts shorter than this one.
Pick the largest of the cells that remain, then count this post itself: max, then + 1.
